extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (educators, professionals, and professional associations)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for public relations as a profession, covering education/curriculum, accreditation and membership requirements, ethics and fiduciary duties, research and the body of knowledge, organizational roles, and the Page Principles for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRIA full professional membership criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals are required to meet strict criteria for full professional membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These include a PRIA-accredited tertiary qualification and a minimum of three years of full-time practice, or a minimum of five years of full-time experience. All members are required to make a personal, written commitment to a stringent Code of Ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRIA Registered Consultancy status
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for an agency to achieve Registered Consultancy status with PRIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency principal must be a full professional member of the PRIA. Consultancy members are bound by the Code of Ethics and an additional Code of Practice covering client relations, fees and income, and general practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum: Theory, Origin, Principles, and Professional Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Undergraduate public relations programs should teach the nature and role of public relations, history and development, theories and principles underlying practice, and societal forces affecting the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coursework should cover the theoretical foundations that inform professional practice and sensitize students to external societal influences on the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum: Public Relations Ethics and Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should include instruction in codes of ethics and standards of practice and relevant legal and regulatory compliance issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics include ethical issues and trends toward greater organizational transparency and legal issues such as privacy, defamation, copyright, workplace diversity, product liability, and financial disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum: Public Relations Research, Measurement, and Performance Evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Training in quantitative and qualitative research designs, tools, and techniques relevant to PR practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes public opinion polls, surveys, experiments; fact-finding and applied research; observation and performance measurement; social, communication, and employee audits; issue tracking; focus groups and interviews; use of external research services and consultants; media clipping and analysis; and historical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum: Public Relations Planning and Management
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction in techniques and models for setting goals and designing strategies and tactics for PR programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers segmenting publics, message design, analyzing problems and opportunities, communicating with top management, budgeting, contingency planning for crises, managing issues, developing timetables and calendars, and assigning authority and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum: Public Relations Writing and Production
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses on communication theory and production across media and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes mass, interpersonal, employee, and internal communication; new and emerging communication technologies; organizational communication and dynamics; communication with diverse audiences and across cultures; persuasion; controlled versus uncontrolled communication; and feedback systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting curriculum and experiential learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Core courses should be supported by internships, tactical courses, and directed electives in supporting disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission advised a public relations internship and coursework focusing on tactical implementation (e.g., writing or campaigns class), plus directed electives in business management, marketing, sociology, public administration, political science, and international business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing education and maintenance of competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must engage in continuing education to keep skills and knowledge current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations such as PRSA and IABC require or encourage members to earn continuing education units (CEUs) through professional development seminars and workshops. Continuing education demonstrates commitment to lifetime learning and competent service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for research and advancement of the body of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals and organizations are obligated to support research that advances the profession's knowledge base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text names bodies such as the Institute for Public Relations (IPR), IABC Research Foundation, PRSA Foundation, Arthur W. Page Center, and the Plank Center that fund, disseminate, and recognize scholarly work; practitioners should contribute to and use this research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific approach to public relations problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations problems should be approached methodically and grounded in research-driven theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The profession requires understanding based on a body of knowledge developed through extensive research — 'Nothing is more practical than a good theory.' Practitioners must approach problems as rigorously as other management disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of professional associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional associations should promote ethics, accreditation, professional development, and the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associations publish journals and resources, enforce codes of conduct, offer accreditation and awards, mentor junior members, sponsor research and conferences, and provide continuing education to strengthen professional standards and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur W. Page Principle: Tell the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Be truthful and provide an accurate picture of the organization's character, ideals and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the public know what's happening and ensure communications reflect the organization's true nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur W. Page Principle: Prove it with action
rubrics_metrics.description: Public perception is determined primarily by actions, not words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public perception is determined 90 percent by what an organization does and 10 percent by what it says; claims should be backed by consistent actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur W. Page Principle: Listen to the customer
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand public wants and needs and keep decision makers informed about public reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To serve the company well, monitor and report public reaction to products, policies, and practices; internal communication of public feedback is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur W. Page Principle: Manage for tomorrow
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate public reaction and eliminate practices that create difficulties; generate goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan proactively to avoid foreseeable problems and develop practices that build long-term public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur W. Page Principle: Conduct PR as a management function
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat public relations as central to corporate strategy and policy-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No corporate strategy should be implemented without considering its public impact; PR professionals should be able to serve as policymakers handling a wide range of communications activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur W. Page Principle: Realize a company's character is expressed by its people
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees' words and deeds shape the strongest opinions about an organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate communications should support employees to be honest, knowledgeable ambassadors to customers, shareowners, and public officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur W. Page Principle: Remain calm, patient, and good-humored
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain composure and consistent, reasoned attention to information and contacts, especially during crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cool heads communicate best in crises; groundwork laid by calm, patient engagement helps produce 'public relations miracles' despite fast news cycles and watchdog scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics, self-policing, and fiduciary obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals should follow applied ethics codified in codes of conduct, engage in self-policing, and honor fiduciary duties to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codes of ethics guide practice and provide a basis for enforcement and sanctions; fiduciary relationships require acting in clients' best interests and maintaining confidentiality. Self-policing protects clients and the profession's public trust and privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social responsibility and societal impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is judged by its impact on society and has obligations to promote ethical discourse and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value to society is enhanced when PR (1) promotes free, ethical competition of ideas, (2) reveals sources and goals of participants, and (3) enforces high standards. Value is diminished when PR (1) suppresses competition, (2) hides true sources of efforts, or (3) leaves incompetent or unethical practice unchallenged. Positives include improved professional conduct, organizational responsiveness, public interest service, mediation in a segmented society, and promotion of human welfare. Negatives include promoting special interests at the public's expense, cluttering communication channels with pseudo-events, and corroding credibility.
